The Standard Body Shapes Defined by BWH
  • Hourglass (X-Shape): The bust and hips are roughly equal in width, paired with a significantly narrower, highly defined waist.
  • Pear / Triangle (A-Shape): The hips are noticeably wider than the bust and shoulders.
  • Inverted Triangle (V-Shape): The bust and shoulders are noticeably wider than the hips.
  • Rectangle / Banana (H-Shape): The bust, waist, and hips are relatively uniform in width, with little to no waist definition.
  • Apple / Oval (O-Shape): The waist is wider than the bust and hips, often featuring a more rounded midsection.

In the context of 3D scene representation and multi-camera optimization, referencing a BVH refers to a Bounding Volume Hierarchy rather than the motion-capture format. 
When positioning optimal 3D camera viewing cones to cover specific point clusters (derived via algorithms like k-means clustering), a BVH acts as an acceleration structure to prune empty 3D space, calculate spatial intersections, and evaluate visual coverage efficiently. 
📐 Why a "Cone" Matters over a Standard Perspective Frustum
In multi-view geometric optimization, a standard 4-sided perspective frustum adds computational complexity when calculating spatial volume intersections. A cone simplifies this math drastically:

  • Isotropic Field of View: A cone provides an omnidirectional, rotationally symmetric angular constraint. When positioning optimal 3D camera viewing cones to cover specific point clusters (derived via algorithms like k-means clustering), a BVH acts as an acceleration structure to prune empty 3D space, calculate spatial intersections, and evaluate visual coverage efficiently.
📐 Why a "Cone" Matters over a Standard Perspective Frustum

Simplified Intersection Rules: Testing whether a cluster or an object bounded by a sphere intersects a camera frustum requires complex plane-separation tests. 🌐 The Role of BVH in This Context
If you are placing camera cones based on k-means clusters in a dense or complex 3D environment, a BVH organizes the scene's geometry (or the cluster data points themselves) into a hierarchical tree of simple bounding volumes (like Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes - AABB, or Bounding Spheres).

📐 Optimal Camera Cone Placement for Egocentric Tracking
When headset-mounted or body-mounted cameras are pointing downward and inward to track your

limbs (Egocentric/Inside-Out Body Tracking), a major challenge is self-occlusion (e.g., your chest blocking the view of your hands). 
Using the K-means approach coupled with a Body BVH optimizes camera placement like this:

on-atomic="" jsaction="click:&hRq7P_c7|ZUljYd" data-processed="true"> 
  1. Primitive-to-Primitive Intersection: Instead of raytracing thousands of points on a clothing mesh, the system models limbs as simplified BVH capsules or boxes. Testing if an inside-out camera's viewing cone captures a hand reduces to checking the overlap between the cone primitive and the Hand Capsule Node in the BVH. 
  2. Dynamic K-Means Centroids: If you are configuring a custom rig with multiple small body-worn sensors, K-means clusters the dense point-cloud data generated only by the limb surfaces. The centroids of these clusters dictate exactly where to anchor and aim the camera cones to ensure the hands and feet never slip out of the tracking volume, regardless of how the body deforms.

  • Continuous Pruning: As the body moves, the hierarchy updates. If the "Upper Left Capsule" (the upper arm) swings in front of the camera cone, the BVH tree instantly flags that all child nodes (forearm, hand) under that branch are occluded along that viewing axis, skipping heavy geometric sorting.

When headset-mounted or body-mounted cameras are pointing downward and inward to track your limbs (Egocentric/Inside-Out Body Tracking), a major challenge is self-occlusion (e.g., your chest blocking the view of your hands).

Using the K-means approach coupled with a Body BVH optimizes camera placement like this:
Primitive-to-Primitive Intersection: Instead of raytracing thousands of points on a clothing mesh, the system models limbs as simplified BVH capsules or boxes. Testing if an inside-out camera's viewing cone captures a hand reduces to checking the overlap between the cone primitive and the Hand Capsule Node in the BVH.

Dynamic K-Means Centroids: If you are configuring a custom rig with multiple small body-worn sensors, K-means clusters the dense point-cloud data generated only by the limb surfaces. The centroids of these clusters dictate exactly where to anchor and aim the camera cones to ensure the hands and feet never slip out of the tracking volume, regardless of how the body deforms.

Continuous Pruning: As the body moves, the hierarchy updates. If the "Upper Left Capsule" (the upper arm) swings in front of the camera cone, the BVH tree instantly flags that all child nodes (forearm, hand) under that branch are occluded along that viewing axis, skipping heavy geometric sorting.
